title: Chevra Kadisha: True Kindness
hookLine: volunteers who prepare the body for burial
carry: kindness to the dead is true kindness

lines: DEAL KINDLY AND TRULY WITH ME.
HE CAN NEVER SAY THANK YOU.
cards: "Deal kindly and truly with me." Jacob says it near the end of Genesis, old and dying in Egypt, to his son Joseph. His request is specific: don't bury me here.
Carry me home, and lay me with my fathers. Joseph swears he will. Notice what Jacob asks for.
Not money, not a blessing. A burial done right, by someone he trusts, after he can no longer say thank you. Jewish communities built a whole institution around that request.

teach.b: It's called the chevra kadisha. Chevra means a society, a group of companions; kadisha is Aramaic for holy. The holy society prepares a body for burial: washing it, dressing it, placing it in the coffin.

They are usually volunteers, ordinary people, a teacher, a dentist, a retired bus driver, who answer the phone when someone dies. Women care for women and men for men. You met Jacob's words in your first year.
The commentator Rashi, reading them, says kindness done for the dead is true kindness, chesed shel emet, because the one receiving it can never repay. No thanks, no favor returned, no one to impress.
At the end of Deuteronomy, Moses dies on a mountain, and the text says he was buried there, and that no one knows his grave. The rabbis read it as God himself burying Moses.
So, they teach, as God buries the dead, so should you.
The holy society does what the tradition calls divine work, with rubber gloves and a basin.
Some societies keep a yearly day of their own, linked to the memory of Moses, with a fast and then a meal together. The rest of the year, the work is quiet.
A society is holy not because of who joins, but because of what it does for people who can't ask.

how: Jewish communities may have a chevra kadisha, a burial society of volunteers who prepare the body for burial, with women caring for women and men for men; some also arrange the shemira and help the family with the funeral.

o: a group that raised money for the Temple
the rabbis who lead a synagogue's prayers
volunteers who prepare the dead for burial

s: the chevra kadisha is a paid professional staff
its members are usually volunteers from the community.
women prepare women and men prepare men
the society cares for each person with that modesty.
Rashi calls kindness to the dead 'true' because it is repaid later
it is true kindness because the one receiving it can never repay.

games.q: Jacob is dying in Egypt. he calls Joseph. what does he ask for?
o: to be buried with his fathers, not in Egypt.
a final feast for the family.
games.why: he asks Joseph to deal kindly and truly with him and carry him home for burial, a kindness he can never repay.

practice: Bring to mind people who do work few people see: hospice volunteers, night-shift nurses, whoever washed the dishes at the last funeral you went to. Picture one of their faces and thank them silently, by name if you know it.
If you pray, you can pray for them.
